name: The Monophysite controversy (one nature)
plain_explanation: The opposite theological error to Nestorianism: the view that Christ has only a single (divine) nature rather than two distinct natures, human and divine, in one person.
precise_definition: The doctrine, condemned as heretical at the Council of Chalcedon (451), that Christ possesses only one nature rather than two natures (human and divine) united in one Person, which the Chalcedonian formula affirmed as orthodox.
why_it_mattered: Egypt adopted Monophysitism almost to a man, and the heresy spread up the Nile into Abyssinia; like Nestorianism in Syria, it weakened Byzantine religious unity and, Russell notes, facilitated the later Arab conquest of Egypt.
historical_origin: Emerged at a synod at Ephesus in 449, after Cyril's death, which Pope Leo secured the overturning of at the Council of Chalcedon in 451.
examples: Mussolini's later citation of Abyssinian Monophysite 'heresy' as a pretext for conquest, noted by Russell as a modern echo
influence_on_later_thinkers: Remained the doctrine of the Egyptian (Coptic) and Ethiopian churches into the modern period.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological, with lasting political consequences for Byzantine control of Egypt and Abyssinia.
